newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada corporate profits surge in fourth quarter.
newsitem.headline: Canada corporate profits surge in fourth quarter.

text.p: Canadian corporate profits surged in the fourth quarter of 1996, buoyed by an improving domestic economy, and economists expect more growth this year.

"The domestic side of the economy has started to pick up, so the corporate earnings environment is quite favorable," said economist Rob Palombi at Toronto-based economic analysis firm MMS International.
"The corporate profitability numbers should look really healthy throughout most of 1997," he added.
Fourth-quarter earnings of the 159 companies in Reuters' first quarterly survey rose 43.7 percent to C$5.83 billion ($4.29 billion) from the same period a year earlier.
Revenues from the companies, which represent the bulk of the Toronto Stock Exchange's key 300 composite index, rose 9.5 percent to C$106.1 billion ($78 billion) in the same period.

The profit spike was exaggerated by almost C$824 million ($606.1 million) in restructuring charges posted by Canadian Pacific Ltd. in 1995. When CP was excluded, 1996 fourth-quarter profits before extraordinary items rose a more modest 10.7 percent.
Companies in nine of the 14 sector subindexes of the TSE 300 saw a year-over-year increase in quarterly profits, pushed by increased consumer spending and long-awaited restructuring benefits.
Consumer products led the pack with a 343.6 percent rise in profits, followed by merchandising, utilities, communications and media, financial services and industrial products.

Nesbitt Burns economist Doug Porter said the contrast between the strong profit gain and the more moderate revenue increase was a sign that Canadian industry was in a more competitive position after the bitter restructuring that marked the early 1990s.

"This is the payoff from years of restructuring and cost-cutting," said Porter. "Their bottom lines are much more highly geared to even a small increase in domestic spending. Merchandisers are a real stellar example of that improvement."
Profits of the merchandising subindex rose 108.7 percent in the quarter, while revenues increased a mere 4.7 percent.
Falling interest rates in Canada also helped boost corporate profits.

"With the sharp drop in rates we had through the year, you would expect that that had a positive effect in general, especially for (companies) on short-term debt," Bunting Warburg strategist George Vasic said.
"Certainly the lower rates assisted the banks to open up the interest margins and they have done very well," he said.
Companies in the financial services subindex saw profits rise 18.7 percent in the fourth quarter on revenue growth of four percent.
But all was not rosy in the fourth quarter, as five subindexes of the TSE 300 saw profits fall. Leading the losers were the resource subindexes, hit by falling or flat commodity prices.
Earnings in the metals and minerals subindex fell 44.6 percent, while gold stock profits halved on flat revenues.

Paper and forestry companies took the most dramatic dive, with earnings falling 155.1 percent to a loss of C$403.8 million ($297 million) from a C$732.3 million ($538.7 million) profit in the same quarter a year ago.
The oil and gas sector was the lone gainer in the resource sector, jumping 280.3 percent on a 28.2 percent increase in revenue and rising oil prices.

"That totally reflects what happened to commodity prices in each one of those sectors," said Porter. "Oil was really the lone wolf in 1996. It was the only commodity to show sustained strength throughout the year."
